name: Kulung
confidence_why: Nothing available says where Kulung word stress falls or whether the language has stress at all: Rai (2015) lists only length, aspiration and intonation as Kulung suprasegmentals, Tolsma (1997) and Namkung (1996) give only segment inventories, and Tolsma's full grammar (1999/2006) and Holzhausen's 1973 phonological survey could not be consulted.

new_statements.translation: 3.1.2 Suprasegmental sounds of Kulung — Sounds that cannot be pronounced alone and can occur only together with segmental sounds are suprasegmental sounds. These include length, nasalisation, breathiness, aspiration, pitch, intonation, etc. Of these, Kulung has only length, aspiration and intonation as suprasegmental sounds. [p. 48] ... Tolsma wrote a descriptive grammar on the basis of the Kulung spoken in Nepal. According to that study, unlike in other Tibeto-Burman languages, no linguistic distinction in tone is found in Kulung. [p. 24]

Surrounding section (pp. 48-51) read:…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No placement rule is given. The source lists the suprasegmentals that function in (Sikkim) Kulung as only vowel length, aspiration and sentence intonation, i.e. neither pitch/tone nor stress is treated as a distinctive word-level property; it reports Tolsma as finding no tonal contrast. Where (non-contrastive) word stress falls is not stated in any source I could open.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the only prosodic detail is falling intonation in declaratives vs rising in polar questions (p. 50-51).
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is about the inventory of suprasegmental features, not about word-level prominence; intonation examples are sentence-level. Variety: Kulung as spoken in Sikkim, India.
new_statements.identity_note: The two accessible descriptions (Reena Rai 2015 M.Phil., 2021 PhD, Sikkim University) describe Kulung as spoken by the diaspora community in Sikkim, India (data from East/West/North/South Sikkim, 2012-2019); the author notes Sikkim Kulung has voiced aspirates absent from Nepal Kulung. Tolsma's works (1997, 1999, 2006) describe the Chheskam (Cheskam) village variety, Solu Khumbu, Nepal, which is the glottocode's reference variety. Sotang (sota1235?) and Nachering are treated by Tolsma 1997 as Kulung dialects. No separate glottocode for Sikkim Kulung.

sources.note: Sec. 3.1.2 'Kulung suprasegmentals' (p. 48): of the suprasegmentals (length, nasalisation, breathiness, aspiration, pitch, intonation etc.) Kulung has only length, aspiration and intonation; subsections treat length, breathy voice, aspiration, sentence intonation (falling declarative / rising interrogative). p. 24 reports Tolsma: no tonal contrast in Kulung. Stress (balaghat) appears only as item 25 in a generic Chomsky-Halle feature list (p. 67), never predicated of Kulung; no statement of stress placement.
